verses.translation_literal: To the leader, of the sons of Korah, a Maskil.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the one who leads the singing; a song of the sons of Korah, a psalm made to instruct.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is not part of the song but a label on the scroll, and in the Hebrew numbering it counts as verse 1, which is why every verse number in this psalm is one higher than in the KJV. 'The leader' is the temple official responsible for the performance; the sons of Korah were a guild of Levite singers and gatekeepers, descendants of the Korah who rebelled in the wilderness, and a number of psalms (42–49, 84–85, 87–88) were kept in their repertoire. Stage it as a liturgy, not a private lament.

The KJV transliterates 'Maschil' and, like most translations, leaves it unexplained. It is probably from the root 'to have insight, to teach': a song to be pondered, or a skilful composition. The Targum reads it as 'good instruction'. The tradition of Meiri and Malbim hears the psalm as a lesson for a long exile, but nothing in the superscription itself says so.

philological_notes.note: 'To the leader/overseer'; the root has a sense of preeminence and supervision, hence the director of the temple music. The traditional 'chief musician' is a reasonable but conjectural explanation of the office.
From 'to have insight'. Either a didactic song or a skilfully made one; the exact sense is not settled.

verses.translation_literal: God, with our ears we have heard; our fathers have recounted to us a deed you did in their days, in the days of old.
verses.translation_dramatic: God, we have heard it with our own ears. Our fathers told it to us, told it and told it again: the deed you worked in their days, in the days long gone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first word is the name, set before everything else, as a worshipper might say 'God' before beginning. Notice the double insistence 'with our ears we have heard' and 'our fathers have recounted': this is knowledge by mouth, passed down at home and at the festival, not by scroll. In a culture that held history in memory, a tale from one's own father carried the weight of testimony; Ibn Ezra and Malbim both stress that a father would not hand on a lie.

The Hebrew repeats a root: 'a deed (po'al) you did (pa'alta)', a cognate pair that the KJV's 'what work thou didst' loses entirely. It sounds like 'a doing you did'. The KJV also supplies 'what' and 'in the times of old' where the Hebrew says literally 'in the days of antiquity'. Rashi, citing the midrash, notes that the sons of Korah were not speaking only for themselves, since they had themselves seen the wilderness, but for the generations that came after.

philological_notes.note: A noun and a verb from the same root: 'a deed you did'. Malbim distinguishes po'al (a new deed beyond the order of nature) from ma'aseh (a thing finished by natural course). The distinction is Malbim's own and not a general rule of the lexicon.
'In days of antiquity'; kedem means both 'east' and 'former time', literally 'what faces forward'. Here it is time, the distant past.

verses.translation_literal: You, your hand, nations you dispossessed, and you planted them [our fathers]; you did harm to peoples, and you sent them away.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, and your hand alone. You tore the nations up from the land, and you planted our fathers in their place. You broke the peoples, and sent them away.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two images of farming and one of war. 'Dispossess' (yarash) is the language of inheritance and land title: you took the nations' estate and gave it to a new tenant. 'Planted' is a gardener's word: the fathers were set into the soil like a vine, to stay. The nations are uprooted and the fathers rooted, in two beats. Radak says planting means standing there for ever, as though rooted in the land.

The opening 'You, your hand' is blunt and without a preposition: ancient commentators (Ibn Ezra, Radak) take it as 'you, with your hand', and the KJV is right to supply 'with thy hand', but the Hebrew drops the word to throw the emphasis on 'you' and 'hand'. The KJV's 'heathen' and 'people' are a softening and a flattening of two different words, goyim and le'ummim; the Hebrew puts 'nations' and 'peoples' side by side. The KJV's 'cast them out' is closer to the sense of the last verb than STEPBible's 'set free', which is a misfit here. Traditionally the dispossessed are the seven Canaanite nations (Rashi); the psalm does not name them. The pronoun on 'planted them' points back to the fathers, not the nations, as the KJV's 'plantedst them' leaves unclear.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of yarash: 'you caused to be dispossessed', 'you drove out'. The same root names inheritance, so the verb frames conquest as a transfer of property, which is why verse 4 repeats it with 'they took possession'.

'You did harm to peoples'. The preposition lamed before 'peoples' is, per Ibn Ezra and Radak, an object marker serving the verb (compare Radak: the word is 'ummim' without lamed). The English 'afflict' of the KJV is a fair rendering.

'And you sent them away', that is, drove them out. Radak and Meiri record a view that the verb here means 'to slay', but 'send away' is the plain sense and matches Ibn Ezra's gloss ('as in vatgareshem').

verses.translation_literal: For not by their sword did they take possession of [the] land, and their arm did not save them; for your right hand and your arm and the light of your face, for you delighted in them.
verses.translation_dramatic: It was not their swords that won the land. It was not their own arms that brought them through. It was your right hand, your arm, the light of your face turned toward them, because you wanted them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speakers are recalling the conquest as every household told it, and the claim is deliberately flat: Israel did not win its land by weapons. The verse is built as a pair of denials followed by a pair of affirmations, and the actors should let the pivot, 'for your right hand', land like a door opening. The right hand was the hand that held the sword, so the poem hands the warrior's own tool to God and leaves Israel's sword empty. The weapons in the first half are human; the limbs in the second half are divine, and the Hebrew uses the same word, zero'a, 'arm', for both: 'their arm' fails, 'your arm' succeeds. Keep that word identical in both places.

The KJV smooths this in small ways. Its 'by their own sword' and 'their own arm' add 'own', which the Hebrew (בְחַרְבָּם, זְרוֹעָם) does not have; that word turns a plain statement into a pointed contrast with self-reliance, when the Hebrew simply says 'their sword' and 'their arm'. It writes 'in possession' for the verb yarashu, which means to take over, to dispossess, and it is the word used elsewhere of inheriting. 'Countenance' is courtly for panim, which is simply 'face', and 'the light of your face' is the old blessing image of a king or deity looking kindly on someone; a ruler's shining face meant favour and a dark one meant danger. The KJV's closing 'thou hadst a favour unto them' makes the last clause a matter of manners; ratsitam is warmer, 'you took pleasure in them', and the verse ends on that bare reason: there is none beyond the delight. Note too the archaic poetic form lamo, 'to them', which the KJV does not mark. Radak reads the doubled 'right hand and arm' as one idea said twice, and the right hand as the hand that does the work and the fighting.

philological_notes.note: The same noun, 'arm', is used for the people's failed strength and for God's effective strength, set against each other by only the suffix. In English keep 'arm' in both places so the contrast is audible.
'The light of your face': God's face turned toward someone, an image of favour. Radak says the light comes to them from God's face, since rescue is likened to light and trouble to darkness.
'You took pleasure in them': the reason given is God's own delight, with no merit offered. Rashi and Metzudat Zion gloss it simply as a word of ratson, favour or will.

verses.translation_literal: You, he, my king, O God: command the victories of Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are he, my king, O God. Speak the word, and let Jacob have his victories.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns on this verse from telling to asking, and from 'we' to 'I'. 'You are he' (atah hu) is an emphatic, almost liturgical formula: you, and no other. The KJV's 'Thou art my King' drops the 'he' and cuts the stress. The speaker is a single voice, but it speaks for the people: Radak and Meiri note that Scripture moves between 'I' and 'we' when a nation speaks.

A king commands, so 'command' is the royal verb: let your word alone produce the victory, as a king's order sends out an army. Radak links it to 'for he will command his angels concerning you' (Ps 91:11). 'Victories' is plural, and the Hebrew is the plural of abstraction, 'full deliverance'; the KJV 'deliverances' is correct. 'Jacob' is the people, the same name as the founder, so it also recalls the God of the fathers in verse 2.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of 'to command': the king's order. Meiri takes it as a verbal noun ('you were the one who commanded'), but the imperative, as in the KJV, is the plain sense.
Plural of yeshu'ah, 'deliverance, victory'; the plural of fullness, 'complete salvation'.

verses.translation_literal: By you our adversaries we gore; in your name we trample those rising against us.
verses.translation_dramatic: Through you we gore our enemies like bulls. In your name we trample them under our feet, every one that rises against us.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the prayer of the last verse the voice swings from asking to boasting, and the boast is borrowed: every verb is 'by you' and 'in your name'. The two halves open with the same little preposition, be-, 'by you' and 'in your name', and the actors should hit it the same way both times, as if the singer were repeating a vow. The imagery is animal and physical. Nenaggeach is the verb for an ox's goring, a bull lowering its horns, and nabus is treading: stamping down, as grapes or mud or a fallen enemy are trodden. Rashi on Psalm 44:6 glosses nabus with 'to trample and tread' and ties it to Ezekiel 16:6 ('trodden in your blood'), Proverbs 27:7 and Zechariah 10:5, where warriors tread the mud of the streets; Metzudat Zion on the same verse takes nenaggeach as a word of goring and nabus as treading.

The KJV's 'push down' tames the goring: the Hebrew is the charge of a horned animal, not a shove. Its 'will we', in both clauses, fixes the verbs in the future, while the Hebrew imperfects can as well describe what the people always do with God's help; ASV and Webster copy that future. 'That rise up against us' is right for the participle kamenu, but the verse says 'those rising', a plain description of enemies, and the sense of hostility comes from Radak's remark that they are called qamim because they rise against a person for harm. 'In your name' matters: the name stood for God's presence and authority, and a battle fought in it was understood as God's own fight, not a charm. The setting is a defeated people who are speaking of strength they have not got at this moment, and the actor should play the boast with some strain.

philological_notes.note: To gore, used of a horned animal. Metzudat Zion glosses it as a word of goring. The English 'push down' of the KJV loses the animal.
To trample, tread down. Rashi: 'we trample and tread our enemies', citing Ezekiel 16:6, Proverbs 27:7 and Zechariah 10:5. Metzudat Zion: a sense of trampling and treading.
'In your name': the name stands for God's presence and authority. Metzudat David says the line repeats the thought of the first half in other words.

verses.translation_literal: For not in my bow do I trust, and my sword does not save me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I do not put my trust in my bow. My sword will not save me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice drops from the crowd to a single soldier. Ibn Ezra hears here the voice of the archer from among the multitude; Radak says the speaker uses the singular 'by way of the whole'. Either way, play it as one warrior speaking for the many, a quiet line after the loud one. 'Bow' and 'sword' are the two tools of the ancient soldier: one for killing at a distance, one at arm's length. A composite bow was the most expensive weapon of the age, and a man who says he does not trust it is giving up his greatest asset.

The KJV's 'will not trust' and 'shall my sword save me' turn the Hebrew's statement of present fact into a future vow. The Hebrew is simple present: 'I do not trust'. The link back to verse 4 is exact: the same verb 'to save' (yasha') that was denied to 'their arm' is denied to 'my sword'. The speaker takes the ancestors' lesson as his own.

philological_notes.note: 'I trust, I rely'. The root denotes confident security; the KJV's 'will not trust' makes a future vow, but the form is an ongoing present.

verses.translation_literal: For you have saved us from our foes, and those who hate us you have put to shame.
verses.translation_dramatic: It was you who saved us from our foes. It was you who put to shame the ones who hated us.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the proof offered for the previous claim: not a sword, but a rescue that everyone saw. The Hebrew order puts 'those who hate us' ahead of the verb, which makes the shaming the climax. In a world of honour and shame, the worst thing that can happen to an enemy army is not death but public humiliation, to be shown that the god they mocked was stronger. 'Hate' here is the language of covenant and treaty, where to hate is to be an enemy by status, not a mood.

The KJV's 'But thou hast saved us' is a good rendering, though it adds 'But' for a Hebrew 'for' (ki). The tenses are perfect, completed acts. Ibn Ezra reads this as the confirmation of what the fathers told: we have seen it ourselves. Radak says this includes the deliverance in Babylon, but the psalm itself does not name it.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of bosh: 'you made them ashamed, you put to shame'. Radak explains: a man who plans something and fails is ashamed.

verses.translation_literal: In God we have boasted all the day, and your name for ever we will give thanks. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: All day long we have made our boast in God, and we will give thanks to your name for ever. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half of the psalm ends on a crescendo, with the whole day filled with praise and the whole future with thanks. 'Boast' (halal) is the verb behind 'hallelujah', but here it is the proud word of a person boasting of a patron: not 'we praise', but 'we brag about him'. Radak says they boasted before their enemies, because they had a God who would rescue them, which sets up the sting in the next verse: they have boasted, and now they look foolish. The KJV 'we boast' is the right word, though it turns the completed 'we have boasted' into a habitual present.

The verb in the second half, 'we will praise' (node), is from a different root, yadah, 'to give thanks, to confess openly'. The two halves pair past boasting with future thanks. Selah is a marker of unknown meaning, probably a musical pause or lift: play it as a held silence before the turn. Metzudat David reads it as a promise to give thanks even before the rescue comes.

philological_notes.note: Piel of halal: 'to praise, to boast'. Here it is boasting, in the sense of taking pride in a patron, which Radak applies to speaking before the enemy.
A liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, probably a pause, a musical interlude or a lifting of the voice. It is left untranslated.

verses.translation_literal: Yet you have rejected, and you have humiliated us, and you do not go out with our armies.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet you have thrown us away. You have shamed us. And you no longer march out with our armies.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn. After nine verses of praise the psalm says 'yet', and the mood breaks. Ibn Ezra says it is not enough that you did not save us, but you rejected us. Everything praised in verses 2 to 9 is now set against what the people see. The sequence is brutal: rejected, shamed, abandoned in the field.

The Hebrew for 'rejected' (zanach) is a harsh word of throwing away, of disowning something that was once chosen; the KJV's 'cast off' is good, but 'put us to shame' softens 'you have humiliated us', and the shame here is exactly the shame that was promised to the enemy in verse 8. The roles are reversed: the same God, the same verb of shaming, now aimed at his own people. Radak's reading is that the people had told their enemies that God would rescue them, so now they are doubly ashamed. 'Go out with our armies' is the old language of holy war, in which God marched at the head of Israel's host (as with the ark in the wilderness): the loss is that of the divine commander. Rashi reads the 'yet' as concessive: even if you shame us, we will still thank you.

philological_notes.note: 'You have rejected, thrown off'. A word of disowning, used of God rejecting his people (Ps 60:3, 74:1).
'And you do not go out with our armies': the old image of God marching out with Israel's host. The verb is imperfect, a continuing state.

verses.translation_literal: You make us turn backward from the foe, and those who hate us have plundered for themselves.
verses.translation_dramatic: You turn us back in flight before the enemy, and the ones who hate us strip us bare and carry the spoil home.
verses.directors_commentary:
The people who once gored their enemies now turn their backs. 'Backward' (achor) is the posture of the rout: in ancient warfare, the soldier who turns and runs gets killed from behind. Rashi notes that the verb here is present tense, an ongoing action; the KJV's 'Thou makest us' is correct.

The verb of the second half, 'plundered' (shasu), is the language of the looter after a battle, and the closing 'for themselves' (lamo) is an old poetic form for 'to them', here a pointed 'each man for himself'. Rashi reads it as each man taking his own share of our goods; the KJV 'spoil for themselves' is faithful. Note that 'hate' recurs from verse 8, where those who hate us were put to shame. Now they are the ones plundering. The reversal is exact.

philological_notes.note: 'They have plundered for themselves': the soldiers' share of the loot. Radak and Meiri observe that the stress falls on the first syllable because of the short word lamo which follows.

verses.translation_literal: You give us like sheep of food, and among the nations you have scattered us.
verses.translation_dramatic: You hand us over like sheep for the table, and you have flung us out among the nations.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the shepherd imagery of the psalms turns monstrous. The usual picture is that God is the shepherd who guards his flock; here he is the one who delivers the flock to the slaughter. 'Sheep of food' is literally 'sheep for eating', not sheep kept for wool or lambs, which the owner protects. Meiri draws the contrast: flocks kept for shearing or breeding are cared for, flocks for slaughter are not. So it is a very hard accusation, and the KJV 'appointed for meat' is accurate; but note that 'meat' in 1611 meant food in general.

The second half moves from the battlefield to exile: 'scattered' (zarah) is the same verb as winnowing grain, tossing it to the wind. Rashi offers an Old French gloss for it, and Metzudat Zion cites Malachi 2:3 ('I will scatter dung'). The word 'nations' (goyim) is the same as in verse 3, where God drove the goyim out of the land; now Israel is the one thrown out among the goyim. The mirror image is deliberate: the same word used for the nations whom God planted the fathers among is used for where the children are cast.

philological_notes.note: 'Like sheep of food', that is, sheep destined to be eaten. Meiri contrasts these with flocks kept for shearing or lambing, which their owners protect.
'You have scattered us', as one winnows grain or throws chaff to the wind.

verses.translation_literal: You sell your people for not-wealth, and you did not increase [your wealth] by their prices.
verses.translation_dramatic: You sold your people, and you did not even ask for a price. No silver rang on the scale; no fortune was made. You gave us away as though we were worth nothing at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is bitter irony, not accounting. In the ancient Near East a people could be sold into slavery, and the seller at least got paid; here the speaker says even that dignity is missing. The line is doubled for force: first 'for not-wealth' (בלא הון, literally 'without wealth'), then 'you did not increase by their prices', with the plural 'prices' (מחיריהם) as if each person had their own tag and the tags added up to nothing. Meiri hears it as sarcasm: a seller of even junk at least sets an asking price and lowers it little by little, but God put them out as goods so worthless that no price was named. Radak adds the logic of the metaphor: a seller does not expect the goods to come back, and a seller takes money; God did neither, since He does not need money.

The KJV 'sellest ... for nought' is fair, but it supplies 'thy wealth' without a bracket and turns the second half into a plain accountant's note ('dost not increase thy wealth'). The Hebrew only says 'you did not grow great'. Play the verse as an accusation spoken with a dry, cracked voice: the people are a bargain bin.

philological_notes.note: 'Sell': the legal word for handing people over to another owner, as in Judg 2:14 and Deut 32:30. Here it is a metaphor for abandoning Israel to its enemies. Meiri notes the image: the speaker feels that exile has gone on so long that it looks like a sale, with no hope of return.
Literally 'with-no wealth': a price that is nothing. Metzudat Zion glosses הון as 'great plenty'.

verses.translation_literal: You make us a reproach to our neighbors, mockery and derision to those around us.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now our neighbors point and sneer. We have become their joke, their scorn, the laughter that follows us whichever way we turn.
verses.directors_commentary:
Honor and shame were public property in the ancient world. A people defeated in war was not only conquered; it was laughed at by every neighbor, for a defeated people meant a defeated god. The speaker lists three words for scorn: 'reproach' (חרפה), 'mockery' (לעג) and 'derision' (קלס). Hebrew heaps up near-synonyms here for the sound of a crowd jeering, and the last two are a matched pair, la'ag and keles. Metzudat Zion ties keles to Ezek 22:4. Note the neighbors are not strangers: Metzudat David says they mock because they know the troubles best, being close.

The KJV 'a scorn and a derision' is solid. YLT's 'a scorn and a reproach' repeats 'reproach' and loses the second word. Say the three words with a rising sneer.

philological_notes.note: A paired phrase for scorn, mock-laughter followed by derision. Metzudat Zion glosses קלס as the same sense as לעג and cites Ezek 22:4.

verses.translation_literal: You make us a byword among the nations, a shaking of head among the peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have made us a proverb on the lips of the nations: when they want to name ruin, they say our name. Heads wag as we pass, slowly, from nation to nation.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'byword' (משל) is a saying people use to describe disaster: 'may you end like Israel.' Metzudat David puts it exactly: when great troubles fall on someone, others say he is like the troubles that came upon Israel. The head-shake (מנוד ראש) is a gesture of mockery and contempt, the same sign as in Ps 22:8 and Lam 2:15; it is not the modern 'no'. The play is a chiasm between 'nations' (גוים) and 'peoples' (לאומים), two words for the same crowds. Malbim presses the difference: goyim are the political groupings, le'ummim the peoples with their own religion, so Israel is a proverb in politics and a head-wag in religion.

The KJV 'heathen' is an archaism and a judgment; the Hebrew is the neutral 'nations'. Perform it as a gesture: the whole company turns, slowly shaking their heads.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'a wagging of head', from the root 'to shake, to wander'. The gesture is scorn, not disagreement. Radak understands it as 'they shake their heads over us'.
A byword or proverb used as a comparison for disaster. Metzudat David and Radak both read it as a byword that other nations use for a fallen, humiliated people.

verses.translation_literal: All the day my disgrace is before me, and the shame of my face has covered me,
verses.translation_dramatic: All day long my disgrace stands in front of me, and I cannot look past it. The shame of my own face has pulled over me like a cloak, and I hide inside it.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice changes from 'we' to 'I'. The speaker steps out of the crowd and feels the shame personally; Radak says the singular 'my disgrace' is collective. Two words for shame are used: kelimmah (disgrace given by others) and bosheth (shame felt in oneself). Malbim draws exactly that line, and it is a neat piece of staging: the insult comes in from outside, and the blush rises from inside. 'Before me' (נגדי) places the disgrace as something standing in front of the speaker like a person, and 'covered me' as a garment or a veil over the face. Hebrew reads 'the shame of my face', which the KJV flattens to 'confusion' for kelimmah: that word is 'disgrace, humiliation', not confusion. The BBE 'downfall' is wrong in the other direction. Play it with the head lowered, voice muffled.

philological_notes.note: 'Disgrace, humiliation', the shame that others pour on you. The KJV's 'confusion' is the older sense of being put to confusion, but it now misleads.
'The shame of my face': the blush or the dropped face. Metzudat David reads it as a figure for the many insults covering the speaker.

verses.translation_literal: From the voice of one who taunts and reviles, from the face of an enemy and a self-avenger.
verses.translation_dramatic: I hear the taunting voice, the curse thrown in my face. I see the enemy's eyes, and in them, a man who is out for revenge.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a fragment, with no verb: it names the sources of the shame in verse 16, a voice and a face. The speaker hears (qol, 'voice') and sees (penei, 'face'). The first pair are two kinds of verbal abuse: 'taunts' (חרף) and 'reviles' (גדף), the second of which is stronger and is the word that later Hebrew uses for blasphemy against God. Malbim reads the pair as abuse between people and abuse of the faith. The last word, mitnaqqem, is a reflexive: 'one who avenges himself', someone who acts as if wronged. Meiri reads this as the enemy who taunts in a rage as though Israel had done him harm.

The KJV 'blasphemeth' is plausible; its 'enemy and avenger' loses the reflexive, so the avenger looks like a righteous one. The YLT 'self-avenger' sees it. Deliver it staccato, like blows.

philological_notes.note: 'One who taunts and one who reviles': both participles. Metzudat Zion glosses גדף as contempt; Malbim reads the second as abuse directed at God and the religion.
Reflexive participle: someone who avenges himself, acting like a man who has been wronged. Meiri notes that the taunts come in anger as though Israel had done them harm.

verses.translation_literal: All this has come upon us, and we have not forgotten you, and we have not dealt falsely in your covenant.
verses.translation_dramatic: All of this has fallen on us, and still we have not forgotten you. We have not lied to you. We have not broken faith with your covenant.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns. After the long list of disasters comes the claim of innocence: 'we did nothing to deserve this.' That claim is the real scandal of Psalm 44. The usual covenant logic (Deut 28) says disaster comes from betrayal; the speakers say they are in the clear. Radak notes they say this even while they see Babylon (in his reading) at ease. Metzudat David reads 'we have not forgotten' as 'we did not stop thanking you', and Malbim adds that it was not only the heart: they did not break the covenant of circumcision and Sabbath even under persecution.

The KJV adds 'yet' which makes the verse a polite protest; the Hebrew has only 'and ... and ...', three plain clauses without a connecting word of contrast. 'Dealt falsely' (שקר) is the language of treaty betrayal: lying to a covenant partner. Say it flatly, as if giving testimony in court.

philological_notes.note: 'We dealt falsely in your covenant': to act deceitfully toward a treaty partner. The verb belongs with treaty language (berit), so the claim is one of loyalty as a vassal.

verses.translation_literal: Our heart has not turned back, [nor] have our steps turned aside from your path.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our hearts have not turned away from you, and our feet have not strayed from your road.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speakers claim loyalty in two images: the heart does not turn 'backward' (אחור), and the feet do not 'bend' away from the 'path' (ארח), an old word for a road beaten by travelers. Heart and feet go together: inner devotion, outer conduct. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David all say the 'not' of the first clause carries over to the second, which is why the KJV, ASV and YLT read it as a denial. The grammar alone would give 'and our steps turned aside' (a narrative verb), which is what Malbim takes: the feet sometimes slipped under the weight of exile, but the heart never turned back. It is a sharp reading, though the denial is the better flow.

The KJV 'declined' is now strange English; the Hebrew verb simply means 'bend, turn off'. Play the two halves as a pair, heart and then feet.

philological_notes.note: 'Our steps': a poetic word for the steps of the feet. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'our feet'.
A narrative verb form, but with the 'not' of the first clause understood. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David say the negative serves for both; Malbim reads it as a real lapse.

verses.translation_literal: For you have crushed us in a place of jackals, and covered over us with deep darkness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even though you crushed us in the jackals' country, and drew the black of deep night over our heads, we kept faith.
verses.directors_commentary:
Jackals haunt ruins and wastes, so 'a place of jackals' is a desolate place: the emptied land after the fall. The KJV 'dragons' is a mistranslation; the animal is the jackal (תן), which is why the ASV has corrected it. Do not confuse it with the sea monster (תנין). Ibn Ezra, however, reads 'place of the sea monsters', the bottom of the sea, with 'deep darkness' as the water's dark; others, he says, read the empty land where only jackals and ostriches live. 'Deep darkness' (צלמות) is traditionally read as 'shadow of death' (tsel-mavet), which the KJV follows; many modern scholars read it as a single word for 'deep gloom'. Either way, it is the darkness of the underworld or the grave.

The opening כי is a stumbling block. Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David take it as 'even though' (the force it has in Exod 33:3, as Meiri notes), so the line is concessive: even when crushed, we did not forsake you. The literal layer keeps 'for'; the dramatic layer carries the 'even though'. Deliver it low and slow.

philological_notes.note: 'Jackals', animals of ruins and wilderness (cf. Isa 34:13, Jer 9:10). KJV 'dragons' follows an older confusion with תנינים (sea monsters). Metzudat Zion glosses 'snakes'; Radak treats the jackals as a figure for cruel rulers.
'Deep darkness', traditionally read as 'shadow of death' (צל + מות). Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as darkness; Radak refers it to the gloom of exile.

verses.translation_literal: If we had forgotten the name of our God and spread out our palms to a strange god —
verses.translation_dramatic: If we had forgotten the name of our God, if we had lifted our open hands to some foreign god —
verses.directors_commentary:
This is an oath of innocence, and the sentence runs on into the next verse: the 'if' is answered by verse 22, 'would God not search this out?', as Rashi and Malbim read it. Stage the two verses as one breath, with the challenge hanging until God is named as the witness. The statement 'if we had forgotten the name' picks up verse 18 ('we have not forgotten you'), and 'spread our palms to a strange god' picks up verse 19 (our steps have not turned aside); Ibn Ezra matches the two. Spreading open hands, palms up, is the ancient posture of prayer, and here it is the posture of worshiping another deity, which is the covenant's gravest offense. 'The name of God' means God's whole character, not just a word. Meiri adds that even forced idolatry would count, and Radak says they would sooner die than do it.

The KJV 'stretched out our hands' loses the picture of palms (כפים); it is 'palms', the cupped open hands of prayer. The KJV also ends the verse on a semicolon and leaves the 'if' to dangle into the next verse; the Hebrew pairs them just as closely. Say it with raised hands and a challenge in the voice.

philological_notes.note: 'Spread out our palms': the gesture of prayer, with the palms open and up. Here it is directed to another god. The same gesture is used for prayer to YHWH in 1 Kings 8:38.
'A strange god', one foreign to Israel. Radak sees the temptation to turn to the gods of the oppressors, who seem to prosper.

verses.translation_literal: Will not God search this out? For he knows the secrets of the heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Will God not search this out? He does know. He knows what lies hidden in the heart of every one of us.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speakers appeal to the one witness who cannot be fooled. A human court judges deeds; God also sees 'the secrets of the heart', the hidden things (תעלומות) that no one else can know. The verb 'search out' (חקר) is the verb of a judge's investigation, as in Jer 17:10, which Meiri quotes ('who searches the heart and tests the kidneys'). Radak reads the whole as: if any thought of denying God ever arose in our hearts, God would know.

The KJV 'Shall not God search this out?' is faithful. The BBE 'make search for it' is clumsy. The question is rhetorical: 'of course he will.' Slow down; it is a challenge, not a doubt. Malbim sees an edge: those who were forced to convert and were still put to death were checked, and found secretly loyal.

philological_notes.note: 'Secrets of the heart', literally 'hidden things': what is concealed from every eye but God's. Metzudat Zion derives it from 'concealment'.

verses.translation_literal: For on your account we are killed all the day; we are reckoned like sheep of slaughter.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is for you that we are being killed, all day long, every day. We are counted as sheep, sheep set aside for the butcher.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse that gives the psalm its force. 'On you' (עליך) can mean 'on your account', 'for your sake' or 'because of you'; the speakers claim that the killing is a consequence of their loyalty, not of their sin. Radak and Metzudat David both read it as 'because we would not deny you'. The picture of sheep goes back to verse 12, where they were sold 'like sheep for the table'; here they are 'sheep of slaughter' (צאן טבחה), flocks kept for the knife, not for wool or milk. Radak makes the point exactly: shepherds who keep sheep for slaughter do not feed them to keep them alive. Rashi's gloss is 'sheep of a butcher'.

The KJV 'for thy sake' is right, and 'counted' is fine. 'All the day' means constantly, not literally twenty-four hours. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 8:36, there applied to Christians suffering for the faith. Deliver it without anger, as a plain statement of fact, and let the silence after it work.

philological_notes.note: 'Sheep of slaughter': animals destined for the butcher. Rashi glosses 'sheep of a butcher'; Radak says those who keep them do so not to pasture them and keep them alive.
'On you': because of you, for your sake. It is the center of the claim: loyalty to God is the cause of the suffering. Metzudat David reads it as 'because of reverence for you'.

verses.translation_literal: Awake! Why do you sleep, my Lord? Wake up! Do not reject [us] for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Wake up! Why do you sleep, my Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not cast us off for good.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speakers shout at God as one would shout at a sleeping watchman. The accusation is stunning: 'Why do you sleep?' Ibn Ezra offers two readings: God looks asleep because He has not saved them, or it is the enemy who says 'perhaps he sleeps, and will wake'. Meiri says God's care has been withdrawn so that He is like one asleep. The two verbs, 'awake' (עורה) and 'wake yourself' (הקיצה), form a double alarm, the second form being stronger.

This would have shocked an ancient audience, and there is an irony. In 1 Kings 18:27 Elijah mocks Baal, saying 'perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened', because a god who sleeps is no god. Here the faithful accuse YHWH Himself of what only idols do. The accusation is a prayer, not a denial: they only dare to say it because they are sure He is there. The KJV 'cast us not off' is fine, though 'arise' for the second verb weakens the hammered repetition. 'Sleepest' and 'thou' are antique, and the Hebrew is blunt, a command and a question. Play it at full voice, then break on 'for ever'.

philological_notes.note: Two commands to wake, one for rousing oneself and one for waking from sleep. The double imperative makes an urgent call.
'Reject, cast off'. Metzudat Zion glosses 'abandon'. The word is used for a rejection that is final, hence 'for ever' after it.

verses.translation_literal: Why do you hide your face, do you forget our affliction and our oppression?
verses.translation_dramatic: Why? Why do you turn your face away? Why do you forget our affliction, forget how hard we are pressed?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the peak of the protest. After the people said that God had sold, scattered and shamed them, they ask the question of the whole psalm: why? In the ancient world a god's "face" was his turned-toward presence, the face of a king who grants an audience or a blessing (compare the priestly blessing, Num 6:25-26). To hide the face is to refuse to look, and so to refuse to act. Ibn Ezra and Radak give the two possibilities the question holds: either you hide your face so as not to see what the enemy does, or you saw and forgot. Radak adds that "the Torah spoke in the language of men": this is how a worshipper has to talk, and not a claim about God's body.

The KJV and ASV insert "and" between "hidest thou thy face" and "forgettest", which turns two cries into one long sentence. The Hebrew sets the two verbs side by side: "you hide... you forget", with the second one as a rebuke. The final pair of nouns, "affliction" and "oppression", comes from the vocabulary of Israel in Egypt: ʿonî is the "affliction" that God saw there (Exod 3:7), and laḥaṣ is the "oppression" he saw at the end (Exod 3:9). So the question is also this: the God who saw and did not forget in Egypt, why not now? The BBE's "cruel fate" loses that echo. Say the last word as if it hurt.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of סתר: to hide, conceal. 'Hiding the face' is a standard way in the psalms to describe God's absence and anger (compare Ps 13:2, 27:9, 88:15). Here it is a question, so it is a charge brought against God.
Noun 'pressure, oppression', from the verb 'to squeeze, press'. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'a matter of pressing'. It is the word of Exod 3:9, where God says he has seen it.

verses.translation_literal: For our soul has sunk down to the dust; our belly has clung to the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For we are brought low: our very life has sunk into the dust, and our bellies cling to the ground, and we cannot rise.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the speech turns from accusation to a picture, and the picture is a body flat on the ground. Do not play it as a metaphor only. A defeated people, beaten in battle or prostrate in mourning, lay on the earth and put dust on their heads; the same posture is the posture of a man in total supplication. Meiri and Radak add a detail you can act: a man who falls puts out his hands to hold himself up, and if his hands give way, his belly lies on the ground. This is the last stage of falling, where there is nothing left to catch you.

The Hebrew uses nefesh, "soul", and beṭen, "belly", side by side, so that the inner and the outer person are both down: the whole self from throat to stomach. Malbim reads the two halves as the exile of the soul and the exile of the body. The KJV's "our soul is bowed down" is sound but polite; the ASV and BBE change "belly" to "body", and so lose the plain, earthy word that the psalmist chose. Nefesh is not an immortal part of a person as in later English: it is the breathing, hungry, throat-and-life self, and here it is pressed into the dust, which is also the place the dead go.

philological_notes.note: 'Has sunk down, been bowed down', a perfect expressing a state reached. Metzudat Zion ties it to the notion of bending and bowing. It describes the posture of someone crouched or prostrate.
'Our belly', the front of the body, the womb in other places. Ibn Ezra takes it as 'the body'; Malbim as the body's exile. The word is physical and low, and it is down at the ground.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, a help for us, and redeem us for the sake of your covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise up! Come to our help, and ransom us: not for what we have earned, but for the sake of your own steadfast love.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long complaint comes one short command, a single imperative stressed on its last syllable (Radak: milra): "Arise!" This is the language of the old war cry (compare Num 10:35, "Arise, O YHWH"), and it is also the opposite of the posture in the last verse: they are on the ground, so God is asked to stand. The people cannot rise by themselves, so they ask the One who can.

The last words are the turning point of the whole psalm. The people have said before (verses 18-23) that they have not been false to the covenant, and they do not now ask to be rescued because they deserve it. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David all say this about the closing phrase: not through the power of our deeds, but for the sake of your ḥesed. Malbim even says "even though we have no merit". Ḥesed is not the KJV's soft "mercies", plural: it is covenant loyalty, the faithful commitment of the stronger party to the weaker, and the thing God swore. The verb pdh, "redeem", is the language of ransom: the price paid to free a slave or a firstborn, and here again of the Exodus. KJV's "for thy mercies' sake" is fine, but the ASV's "lovingkindness" is a Coverdale word that obscures how legal this is. The people end on the one thing they can plead: your own name and your own promise.

philological_notes.note: 'Help', with a final ה. Radak says it is 'like לעזרתה', 'for the help of'; Ibn Ezra offers a second reading, 'arise, you who were a help to us'. The sense is the same: be our help.
Loyal love owed within a covenant. The people appeal to God's own character and not to their own claim.
